session.question: How are coronary artery calcifications associated with complications?
session.answer:
Coronary artery calcifications are associated with a higher risk of adverse outcomes and complications. In level-1 trauma patients, calcification seen on routine CT was independently associated with worse in-hospital outcomes; left main coronary artery calcification increased the odds of any complication, and a greater number of calcified coronary arteries showed a trend toward more complications and was significantly associated with an adverse discharge condition. The main complications observed were pneumonia and delirium. (kobes2022cardiovascularparameterson chunk 1)

In symptomatic patients referred for cardiac CT, higher absolute coronary artery calcification score predicted all-cause mortality over follow-up, indicating that greater coronary calcification corresponds to worse prognosis and increased risk of death. MESA percentile-based adjustment did not improve prediction over absolute calcification burden. (siegersma2022coronarycalcificationmeasures chunk 1)

Overall, the context supports coronary artery calcification as a marker of higher complication risk and poorer prognosis, particularly for in-hospital complications in trauma and long-term mortality in symptomatic cardiac patients. (kobes2022cardiovascularparameterson chunk 1, siegersma2022coronarycalcificationmeasures chunk 1)

pqac-ff56b39f: The study found that coronary artery calcification seen on routine trauma CT was independently associated with worse in-hospital outcomes. Specifically, left main coronary artery calcification increased the odds of developing any complication (OR 3.9, 95% CI 1.7–8.9). An increasing number of calcified coronary arteries showed a trend toward association with complications and was significantly associated with an adverse discharge condition. The main clinical complications observed were pneumonia and delirium. Pulmonary emphysema and aortic calcifications were not associated with complications. Overall, coronary artery calcification may help identify trauma patients at higher risk for adverse prognosis and in-hospital complications.
From Tim Kobes, Arthur A. R. Sweet, IJsbrand T. Klip, Roderick M. Houwert, Wouter B. Veldhuis, Luke P. H. Leenen, Pim A. de Jong, and Mark C. P. M. van Baal. Cardiovascular parameters on computed tomography are independently associated with in-hospital complications and outcomes in level-1 trauma patients. European Journal of Trauma and Emergency Surgery, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00068-022-02168-7, doi:10.1007/s00068-022-02168-7.

pqac-5fae7159: This study examined whether coronary artery calcification score (CACS) and MESA percentiles predict adverse outcomes in 4,985 symptomatic patients referred for cardiac CT. Over a median 4.4-year follow-up, 116 patients died (all-cause mortality). The key clinical finding was that absolute CACS predicted mortality with moderate accuracy, indicating that higher coronary calcification is associated with worse prognosis and increased risk of death in symptomatic women and men. MESA sex-, age-, and race/ethnicity-specific percentiles did not improve prediction over absolute CACS. Adding degree of stenosis may slightly improve mortality prediction in women, but not in men.
From Klaske R Siegersma, Floor Groepenhoff, Anouk L M Eikendal, Willemijn J op den Brouw, Tim Leiner, Yolande Appelman, Igor I Tulevski, G Aernout Somsen, N Charlotte Onland-Moret, Leonard Hofstra, and Hester M den Ruijter. Coronary calcification measures predict mortality in symptomatic women and men. Open Heart, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1136/openhrt-2022-002005, doi:10.1136/openhrt-2022-002005.

It reports that coronary artery calcification on routine CT was independently associated with in-hospital complications and an adverse discharge condition. Specifically, left main coronary artery calcification increased the odds of any complication (OR 3.9, 95% CI 1.7–8.9), and a greater number of calcified coronary arteries trended toward more complications and was significantly associated with worse discharge outcome. Pulmonary emphysema and aortic calcifications were not associated with complications.
From Tim Kobes, Arthur A. R. Sweet, IJsbrand T. Klip, Roderick M. Houwert, Wouter B. Veldhuis, Luke P. H. Leenen, Pim A. de Jong, and Mark C. P. M. van Baal. pqac-838aa3e7: The excerpt discusses lower-limb arterial calcification in hemodialysis patients, not coronary artery calcification specifically. It reports that higher arterial calcification scores were associated with worse long-term clinical outcomes, including cardiovascular events, mortality, and limb amputations. In univariate analyses, calcification scores plus factors like CRP, low albumin, age, diabetes, ischemic heart disease, and critical limb-threatening ischemia were linked to 3-year and 10-year outcomes. Multivariate analysis found superficial femoral artery calcification independently predicted 10-year cardiovascular events and amputations, and Kaplan–Meier analysis showed higher calcification levels were associated with cardiovascular events and mortality. This suggests calcification marks higher complication risk and poorer prognosis.
From Takayasu Ohtake, Ayaka Mitomo, Mizuki Yamano, Toshihiro Shimizu, Yasuhiro Mochida, Kunihiro Ishioka, Machiko Oka, Kyoko Maesato, Hidekazu Moriya, Sumi Hidaka, Milanga Mwanatambwe, and Shuzo Kobayashi. Impact of arterial calcification of the lower limbs on long-term clinical outcomes in patients on hemodialysis. Journal of Clinical Medicine, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm12041299, doi:10.3390/jcm12041299.

pqac-52bae320: This excerpt is a case report about pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) and detailed coronary artery disease assessment. It notes that intravascular imaging suggested fragmented and calcified elastic fibers in the internal elastic lamina, implying a possible pathophysiology for coronary artery disease in PXE. However, the excerpt does not provide general information about how coronary artery calcifications are associated with complications, prognosis, or adverse outcomes beyond this PXE-specific coronary finding.
From Tomohiro Fujisaki, Masanobu Ishii, Bengo Atari, Tomoyo Matsumura, and Kenichi Tsujita. Pseudoxanthoma elasticum with detailed analyses of coronary artery disease. JACC Case Reports, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaccas.2023.101894, doi:10.1016/j.jaccas.2023.101894.

contexts.context: The excerpt is a meta-analysis comparing PCI vs CABG in diabetic patients with multivessel coronary artery disease. It does not specifically discuss coronary artery calcifications. However, it does report clinically important adverse outcomes and prognosis: PCI was associated with higher all-cause mortality, MACCE, myocardial infarction, repeat revascularization, and cardiac death, while CABG had a higher rate of cerebrovascular accident. Overall, CABG was concluded to be the preferred treatment in eligible diabetic multivessel disease patients because PCI had worse long-term outcomes.

It describes a postoperative coronary artery spasm after aortic valve replacement as a rare but life-threatening complication that can occur even with normal coronary arteries. In the reported case, the patient developed hypotension and ST-segment elevation 19 hours after surgery, angiography showed diffuse 3-vessel spasm, and multiple intracoronary vasodilators failed. The patient ultimately died from prolonged low cardiac function and pneumonia. The text emphasizes that postoperative coronary artery spasm has poor prognosis when refractory to treatment.

session.formatted_answer:
Question: How are coronary artery calcifications associated with complications?

Coronary artery calcifications are associated with a higher risk of adverse outcomes and complications. In level-1 trauma patients, calcification seen on routine CT was independently associated with worse in-hospital outcomes; left main coronary artery calcification increased the odds of any complication, and a greater number of calcified coronary arteries showed a trend toward more complications and was significantly associated with an adverse discharge condition. The main complications observed were pneumonia and delirium. (kobes2022cardiovascularparameterson chunk 1)

In symptomatic patients referred for cardiac CT, higher absolute coronary artery calcification score predicted all-cause mortality over follow-up, indicating that greater coronary calcification corresponds to worse prognosis and increased risk of death. MESA percentile-based adjustment did not improve prediction over absolute calcification burden. (siegersma2022coronarycalcificationmeasures chunk 1)

Overall, the context supports coronary artery calcification as a marker of higher complication risk and poorer prognosis, particularly for in-hospital complications in trauma and long-term mortality in symptomatic cardiac patients. (kobes2022cardiovascularparameterson chunk 1, siegersma2022coronarycalcificationmeasures chunk 1)
